quests.hint: After the latest fashion trend went viral, the same style of trainers appeared in every shop and on every street corner — they were everywhere and nothing special. Which idiom fits?
quests.explanation: 'A dime a dozen' means something is very common, ordinary, and not special or valuable. Example: 'Good intentions are a dime a dozen — what matters is action.' It originates from American English, where a dime (ten cents) once bought twelve of something inexpensive.

quests.hint: When asked which political party she supported, Hannah said she liked policies from both sides and simply could not commit to either one. Which idiom describes her position?
quests.explanation: 'On the fence' means undecided, not committed to either side of an issue. Example: 'I'm still on the fence about whether to accept the job offer.' It comes from the image of sitting on a fence between two areas, not choosing a side.

quests.hint: Michael told his coworkers he had just won fifty thousand pounds in a competition, but it was completely made up — he was just joking around to see their reactions. Which idiom describes what Michael was doing?
quests.explanation: 'Pull someone's leg' means to tease or joke with someone in a friendly, playful way. Example: 'He said there was a spider on my shoulder, but he was only pulling my leg.' It suggests harmless teasing, not serious deception.

quests.hint: After failing to submit a critical report on time, the employee received a very serious warning and was told it must never happen again. Which idiom describes his situation?
quests.explanation: 'In hot water' means in trouble or facing a difficult, potentially serious situation. Example: 'She got in hot water for missing the client deadline.' It suggests an uncomfortable situation with real consequences.

quests.hint: After investors rejected every single idea in the business plan, the team realised they needed to abandon their current approach and begin planning entirely from scratch. Which idiom fits?
quests.explanation: 'Go back to the drawing board' means to start over completely after a plan has failed. Example: 'Our product launch flopped, so we had to go back to the drawing board.' It comes from returning to an architect's drawing board to create an entirely new design.
options: go back to the drawing board

quests.hint: With exams only three days away, the students spent every evening at the library reviewing notes and textbooks intensively. Which idiom describes what they were doing?
quests.explanation: 'Hit the books' means to study hard. Example: 'I have a test on Monday, so I need to hit the books this weekend.' It is an energetic, informal expression for serious, focused studying.

quests.hint: To reduce costs on the building project, the contractor used cheaper materials than specified and skipped several mandatory safety checks. Which idiom describes this approach?
quests.explanation: 'Cut corners' means to do something in the quickest or cheapest way, often sacrificing quality or safety. Example: 'You can't cut corners on safety inspections — lives are at stake.' It suggests taking shortcuts that lower the overall standard.

quests.hint: After three days of avoiding the subject, David finally decided to sit down with his parents and tell them the complete, honest truth about what had happened. Which idiom describes his decision?
quests.explanation: 'Come clean' means to confess the truth or admit something you have been hiding. Example: 'She finally came clean about losing the money.' It suggests a move from dishonesty or concealment to openness and honesty.

quests.hint: When Emma arrived at the party, her former best friend refused to say hello, avoided all eye contact, and walked to the other side of the room. What was the friend doing to Emma?
quests.explanation: 'Give someone the cold shoulder' means to deliberately ignore someone, usually as a sign of displeasure or rejection. Example: 'Ever since our argument, she has been giving me the cold shoulder.' It suggests purposefully cold and unfriendly treatment.

quests.hint: The hotel staff stayed late, arranged special meals, organised transport, and went well beyond their normal duties to make every guest completely comfortable. Which idiom describes their effort?
quests.explanation: 'Bend over backwards' means to try extremely hard to please or help someone. Example: 'She bent over backwards to make the new employee feel welcome.' It suggests exceptional, almost uncomfortable effort to accommodate others.

quests.hint: The supervisor who had been rude to her team for years was eventually given a manager who treated her in exactly the same dismissive way. Her team felt it was perfectly fair. Which idiom applies?
quests.explanation: 'Get a taste of your own medicine' means to experience the same unpleasant treatment you have given to others. Example: 'He was rude to everyone for years and finally got a taste of his own medicine.' It implies poetic justice.
options: get a taste of one's own medicine

quests.hint: When the fitness app went viral, every influencer and brand suddenly began promoting it — not out of conviction, but simply because everyone else was doing so. Which idiom describes this behaviour?
quests.explanation: 'Jump on the bandwagon' means to do something because it is popular or fashionable, not because of genuine conviction. Example: 'Companies are jumping on the bandwagon with sustainability claims.' It comes from political parades where people literally climbed onto a band's wagon.

quests.hint: Before the exam results were released, Fatima genuinely hoped with all her heart that she had passed. Which idiom describes her hopeful attitude?
quests.explanation: 'Keep one's fingers crossed' means to hope earnestly for a good outcome. Example: 'Keep your fingers crossed for me — the interview results are announced tomorrow!' It comes from the superstition that crossing fingers brings good luck.

quests.hint: A salesman tried to convince an experienced businesswoman to invest in a suspicious deal using elaborate arguments. She immediately saw through his deception and refused. Which idiom describes her?
quests.explanation: 'Not born yesterday' means experienced enough not to be easily fooled or deceived. Example: 'Don't try to trick me — I wasn't born yesterday.' It suggests a person has lived and learned enough to recognise dishonesty when they see it.

quests.hint: Although the manager's email was polite, Carla sensed from its careful wording that a restructuring was coming — even though nothing was stated directly. Which idiom describes her skill?
quests.explanation: 'Read between the lines' means to understand the hidden or implied meaning in something written or spoken. Example: 'Reading between the lines, I think he wants to leave the team.' It applies when the real message is not stated openly.
options: get a taste of one's own medicine
go back to the drawing board

quests.hint: Despite the school having support services, several students who urgently needed help were never identified or assisted because they were not noticed by the system. Which idiom describes what happened to them?
quests.explanation: 'Fall through the cracks' means to be missed or overlooked by a system designed to help people. Example: 'Some vulnerable children fall through the cracks of the welfare system.' It suggests being lost in a structure that should have caught them.

quests.hint: After months of negotiations, the deal completely collapsed, meaning both companies had to return to the very beginning and restart all discussions from zero. Which idiom fits this situation?
quests.explanation: 'Back to square one' means returning to the very beginning after a plan or effort has failed completely. Example: 'The experiment failed again — we're back to square one.' It originally comes from early board games where landing on a penalty sent players back to the starting square.
options: every cloud has a silver lining

quests.hint: After three years of not speaking following a serious falling-out, two old friends finally met, forgave each other, and decided to put the past behind them. Which idiom describes their decision?
quests.explanation: 'Bury the hatchet' means to end a conflict and make peace with someone. Example: 'The two rival companies finally buried the hatchet and agreed to collaborate.' It comes from a Native American tradition of literally burying weapons as a symbol of peace.

quests.hint: Although losing his job was devastating at first, Carlos used the unexpected free time to launch the business he had always dreamed of, which eventually became a great success. Which idiom reflects the positive side?
quests.explanation: 'Every cloud has a silver lining' means that even negative or difficult situations contain something positive. Example: 'I failed my course, but every cloud has a silver lining — now I know exactly what to improve.' It offers optimism during hard times.
options: every cloud has a silver lining

quests.hint: When the project was cancelled just before launch, all the months of work, money, and effort invested in it amounted to absolutely nothing. Which idiom describes what happened to those resources?
quests.explanation: 'Down the drain' means completely wasted or lost. Example: 'If we don't finish this, all our hard work will go down the drain.' It comes from the image of something valuable disappearing irretrievably into a drain.

quests.hint: When a new employee struggled to understand the sign-in process, a colleague pointed out it was a very simple three-step task that anyone could do. Which idiom could the colleague use?
quests.explanation: 'It's not rocket science' means something is not complicated or difficult to understand. Example: 'The instructions aren't rocket science — just follow the steps in order.' Rocket science is notoriously complex, so this idiom highlights simplicity by contrast.
options: every cloud has a silver lining

quests.hint: Ben volunteered to lead five separate project teams simultaneously and quickly realised he did not have enough time or energy to manage them all well. Which idiom describes his mistake?
quests.explanation: 'Bite off more than you can chew' means to take on more responsibility or work than you are able to handle. Example: 'She bit off more than she could chew by promising to complete four reports in one week.' It suggests overcommitting beyond your own capacity.
options: bite off more than you can chew
get off on the wrong foot

quests.hint: After making serious errors in the financial report, the employee knew she could no longer avoid the consequences and went to speak to her director honestly. Which idiom describes what she had to do?
quests.explanation: 'Face the music' means to accept responsibility for your actions and deal with the consequences, however unpleasant. Example: 'You made the mistake — now you need to face the music.' It suggests bravely confronting the results of your own actions.
options: go back to the drawing board

quests.hint: Having moved from a quiet village to a sprawling megacity, the new student felt completely out of place, unsure how to behave, and deeply uncomfortable in the new environment. Which idiom describes how she felt?
quests.explanation: 'A fish out of water' means a person who is in an unfamiliar or uncomfortable situation where they do not belong. Example: 'At the formal gala, the laid-back artist felt like a fish out of water.' It compares a fish's distress outside water to a person's discomfort in an alien environment.

quests.hint: On his very first day at a new company, the new hire accidentally insulted his manager by joking about a project the manager had personally led. How did their professional relationship start?
quests.explanation: 'Get off on the wrong foot' means to make a bad start to a relationship or situation. Example: 'I got off on the wrong foot with my new flatmate when I played loud music on the first night.' It suggests an unfortunate beginning that creates early problems.
options: get off on the wrong foot

quests.hint: Although the job only required basic customer support, the staff member spent an extra two hours patiently helping a confused elderly customer understand every available option. Which idiom describes her effort?
quests.explanation: 'Go the extra mile' means to put in more effort than what is required or expected. Example: 'He always goes the extra mile for his clients, which is why they keep coming back.' It suggests going beyond what is necessary to deliver truly exceptional results.

quests.hint: After discovering that his colleague had claimed full credit for his work in front of the management team, James wanted to speak to him directly and express his frustration. Which idiom describes what James wanted to do?
quests.explanation: 'Have a bone to pick with someone' means to have a complaint or problem with someone that you want to discuss directly. Example: 'I have a bone to pick with you — you never told me the meeting was cancelled.' It implies confronting someone about a specific grievance.
options: every cloud has a silver lining
have a bone to pick with someone

quests.hint: In casual conversation, a man joked that his ancient car had finally broken down permanently and could never be repaired. Which humorous idiom could he use to describe the car's fate?
quests.explanation: 'Kick the bucket' is an informal, often humorous expression meaning to die, or for something to stop functioning permanently. Example: 'My old laptop finally kicked the bucket — it won't even turn on.' It is typically used in casual speech.
options: get off on the wrong foot

quests.hint: Daniel kept putting off applying for the scholarship, and by the time he finally checked, the deadline had already passed two days earlier. Which idiom describes what happened to him?
quests.explanation: 'Miss the boat' means to miss an opportunity by not acting quickly enough. Example: 'If you don't register today, you'll miss the boat for the early-bird price.' It compares a missed opportunity to arriving at the dock after a boat has already sailed.
options: bite off more than you can chew

quests.hint: The new intern immediately noticed a major error in the quarterly report that three senior analysts had overlooked, and corrected it before it was sent to clients. Which idiom describes this intern?
quests.explanation: 'On the ball' means alert, efficient, and quick to notice or respond to things. Example: 'She's really on the ball — she spotted the error in the contract before it was signed.' It suggests someone who is sharp, attentive, and highly competent.
